title: Everest Statements and Clarity of Purpose
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart makes the case that teacher and student clarity of purpose is foundational and chronically neglected, quoting Greg McKeown's Essentialism on how a lack of clarity causes teams, and classrooms, to waste time and energy on the trivial many. His solution is the Everest Statement, a single sentence answering what is your class all about, which he has helped thousands of teachers draft in workshops. He shares his own statement and several from colleagues across disciplines, flags the two most common drafting failures, too generic and too lifeless, and details practical uses for the statement once written: opening the year, reducing teacher guilt on bad days, anchoring Mini-Sermons, clearing the clouds of confusion mid-lesson, and guiding activity selection so students never do busywork.
points: Stuart's central diagnostic, borrowed from Greg McKeown's Essentialism, is that motivation and cooperation deteriorate when there is a lack of purpose, applying equally to classrooms, faculty meetings, and PLCs.
He identifies two recurring failure modes in early Everest Statement drafts: statements so generic they could apply to any subject, and statements so flat they answer what without ever touching why.
On hard days, Stuart uses his own Everest Statement as an internal permission slip, letting him rest and try again tomorrow if the day's chaos still moved toward the statement's aim.

Because students have a right to never experience busy work, he uses the Everest Statement as a filter for selecting instructional activities, screening out anything that doesn't serve the stated purpose.
quotes: We are not clear on what our classes are for. What's ELA all about? What's science all about? What's physical education all about? We are familiar with what our subject is for, but we're not clear on it.
Clarity of purpose…consistently predicts how people do their jobs….The fact is, motivation and cooperation deteriorate when there is a lack of purpose.
To begin, simply answer this question by hand: What, in a single sentence, is your class all about? What is a summary of all the work your students will do and what you hope that work amounts to?
What you don't want is an Everest Statement that could be used by any person who is working with young people.

On days like these, I can look at my Everest Statement and ask myself, Did we attempt to do any of this work today? If my answer is yes, I can give myself permission to go home and try again tomorrow.
Students have a right to never experience busy work — work designed for the purpose of keeping students busy versus work designed to help them grow toward Everest.
